title: Ocarina

altText: A tiny ceramic ocarina that fits in the palm of a hand, with a small rounded body made of fired clay. It is shown on a plain background.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, culture (Tairona People; Gayraca style), country, classification (Aerophone-Whistle Flute-vessel flute), dimensions, public-domain flag, creditLine, and image URLs read from the record

context: An ocarina is a small wind instrument with a hollow, vessel-shaped body. The Met dates this one to 1300–1500, attributes it to the Tairona People of Colombia in the Gayraca style, and lists ceramic as its medium. It measures only about 5 cm (1 15/16 in.) long, so it could be held in one hand.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny ocarina made of clay. It is so small that it fits in your hand. It was made long ago in Colombia, in South America. It is hollow inside. What do you think happens when someone blows into it?
descriptions.g12: This ocarina is very small, only about five centimeters long. It was made of clay by Tairona people in Colombia more than 500 years ago. It is hollow, so air can move inside. How do you think someone held it?
descriptions.g35: This ocarina was made by the Tairona people of Colombia between 1300 and 1500. It is made of fired clay and is only about five centimeters long, so it fits in the palm. The Met classifies it as a vessel flute, a hollow wind instrument. It is also called Gayraca style. What does its small size tell you about how it might have been made and used?
descriptions.g68: This ceramic ocarina, made by the Tairona people of Colombia between 1300 and 1500, measures only about five centimeters. The Met classifies it as a vessel flute, meaning a hollow clay body with an air passage, and identifies its style as Gayraca. Tairona ceramics are known for a wide range of forms, but the record does not describe what this one represents. How can a tiny object hold so much cultural information, and what do we still not know?
descriptions.g910: This tiny ocarina is attributed to the Tairona People of Colombia and the Gayraca style, and dated 1300–1500. At roughly five centimeters, it shows how ceramics could serve sound as well as vessels or figures. The Met classifies it as a vessel flute but says little about its shape, symbolism or use, so interpretations should stay careful. Think about how a museum label translates a living culture's object into a catalogue entry, and what is lost in that translation.
descriptions.g1112: Catalogued as Tairona, Gayraca style, and dated 1300–1500, this ceramic ocarina is small enough to hold in the hand and leaves much unsaid. The record classifies it as a vessel flute but does not tell us what, if anything, its form depicts, how it was played or what role it had in Tairona society. Scholars piece together such roles from excavations, comparisons with other ceramics and colonial-era sources, each with limits. The object invites reflection on how museums interpret Indigenous works with partial evidence and how living descendants might read them differently.

teacherNote.context: A tiny ceramic ocarina attributed to the Tairona People of Colombia (Gayraca style), dated 1300–1500. The record does not describe its shape, subject or use, so students should only describe what they can see.
directions: Compare an ocarina with a recorder: where does the air go in each?
Pinch a small clay form and discuss how it could be turned into a hollow shape.
Talk about how museums describe objects when only partial information exists.
